props.title: Legion
props.initialSlug: The archangel Michael protects humanity from God's wrath

sections.content: **Legion** (2010) marks a fascinating entry in religious horror, blending apocalyptic themes with action-packed angel warfare. It shares DNA with earlier religious horror films like **The Prophecy** (1995) and **Constantine** (2005), but adds a distinctly militaristic edge. The film's premise - God losing faith in humanity and sending angels to exterminate us - flips traditional divine intervention narratives on their head, similar to how **Dogma** (1999) subverted religious expectations with dark humor.

sections.content: Director Scott Stewart's background in visual effects shines through Legion's action sequences, particularly in Paul Bettany's athletic portrayal of Michael. The film's isolated diner setting creates a siege atmosphere reminiscent of **Night of the Living Dead** (1968), while its possessed humans echo **The Evil Dead** (1981). This combination of religious mythology and horror tropes would later influence films like **Priest** (2011) and **I, Frankenstein** (2014).

The film's treatment of angels as militaristic beings draws from ancient religious texts where angels were warriors, not just messengers. This martial interpretation influenced later works like **Dominion** (2014) and aspects of **Supernatural** (2005-2020). The movie's practical effects and makeup work, especially in the possessed human sequences, harken back to John Carpenter's **Prince of Darkness** (1987). SUBHEAD: Religious Horror Evolution

sections.content: Legion's impact on religious horror helped pave the way for more action-oriented interpretations of biblical mythology. While earlier films like **The Exorcist** (1973) focused on possession and faith, Legion sparked a trend of weaponized religion seen in **Warrior Nun** (2020) and **The Order** (2019). The film's depiction of angels as antagonists particularly influenced **Syfy's Dominion** (2014-2015), a direct sequel series to the movie.
